title: MB8-00797
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Haiti, is appealing against a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting his claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Haiti, is appealing against a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting his claim for refugee protection.
He is not submitting any new evidence in his appeal, nor is he requesting a hearing before the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD).

Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the RAD confirms the RPD's determination, namely, that XXXX XXXX is neither a "Convention refugee" pursuant to section 96 of the IRPA, nor a "person in need of protection" pursuant to section 97 of the IRPA.

In his Basis of Claim Form (BOC Form), the appellant alleges that he left Haiti on XXXX XXXX, 2013, to travel to the Dominican Republic and then to Brazil because he had been threatened and assaulted by his neighbours who were jealous of his success as a XXXX.
The appellant claims that he was the victim of racism and discrimination at his workplace in Brazil when he was abandoned in a remote city by his fellow driver.

The appellant alleges that he witnessed assaults and racism directed at Haitians in Brazil, and therefore decided to leave the country and travel to the United States in XXXX 2016, where he remained until July 2017, when he came to Canada and filed a claim for refugee protection.

The RPD determined that the appellant was excluded under Article 1E of the Convention because he had permanent resident status in Brazil. The RPD further determined that the appellant had access to state protection in Brazil, that he had failed to establish that his fear of returning to Brazil amounted to persecution within the meaning of the Convention, and that he was therefore not a "Convention refugee" or a "person in need of protection."

The appellant is arguing before the RAD that the RPD erred in concluding that he was excluded under Article 1E of the Convention because, in reality, given the hostile and xenophobic conditions that Haitians face in Brazil, their status is not similar to that of Brazilian nationals.
The appellant further argues that the RPD erred by not giving [translation] "any real consideration" to the racism he experienced in Brazil.
For these reasons, the appellant is asking the RAD to set aside the RPD's determination and grant him refugee protection.

The role of the RAD is to review RPD decisions on a correctness standard after conducting its own analysis of the record in order to determine whether the RPD erred as the appellant alleges. The exception to this rule arises when the RPD's findings relate to the assessment of the credibility or weight to be given to the oral testimony, in situations where it enjoyed a meaningful advantage. In these situations, the RAD must apply the reasonableness standard of review (Canada v. Huruglica, F.C.A. No. A-470-14). If I find that the RPD enjoyed a meaningful advantage, I will explain how in my analysis.
paragraphs.heading_before: STANDARD OF REVIEW AND THE RAD'S ROLE

paragraphs.text: In my opinion, the first matter to be determined in the present case is whether the RPD erred in concluding that the appellant's permanent resident status in Brazil grants him rights similar to those of Brazilian nationals and that Article 1E of the Convention therefore applies to him.
In my opinion, the RPD did not err, for the following reasons.

The appellant stated that the discrimination and racism that Haitians face in Brazil is such that even permanent resident status does not grant them rights similar to those of Brazilian nationals. I note that this argument was not invoked by the appellant or his counsel before the RPD, and his counsel did not question him on this subject before the RPD.

In paragraph 13 of the appellant's memorandum, he claims that Haitians who have permanent resident status in Brazil do not benefit from rights similar to those of Brazilian nationals because [translation] "they endure discrimination based on their race and nationality, which affects their ability to benefit from equal access to employment, housing, property rights, education, travel (and) social benefits such as access to medical care and freedom of expression."
In my opinion, nothing in the evidence shows that the appellant made such an allegation.
On the contrary, the appellant testified that he was employed in Brazil and that employers generally prefer to hire Haitians because they are allegedly better employees than Brazilians.
At no point did the appellant allege that he was denied the right to housing, education, travel or social benefits such as medical care or freedom of expression.

The documentary evidence submitted in this file (see Tab 3.4 of the National Documentation Package (NDP) for Brazil dated March 31, 2017), as noted in the RPD's reasons, indicates that permanent residents in Brazil have the right to work, study and have access to social services.

I am therefore of the opinion that the RPD did not err in concluding that the appellant's status in Brazil is essentially similar to that of a Brazilian national and that he is therefore a person referred to in Article 1E of the Convention.

As mentioned above, in paragraphs 16 and 17 of his memorandum, under the heading [translation] "Fear of returning to Brazil," the appellant also argues that the RPD erred by giving "no real consideration" to the racism that he endured in Brazil, and he adds that, [translation] "the panel should have examined the claimant's particular circumstances."

I am not sure that I understand this argument. It is also unclear to me whether this argument pertains to the appellant's fear of returning to Brazil or is a continuation of his previous observation that he should not be excluded under Article 1E of the Convention.

Regardless-and this is the second issue to be decided in this case-I am of the opinion that the RPD did not err in concluding that the appellant's fear of returning to Brazil is not equivalent to a fear of persecution, for the following reasons.

In his BOC Form and in his testimony, there is only one incident that he describes as racist and discriminatory. The appellant alleged that his co-worker abandoned him in a remote city and that he had to find his own way home.

When questioned about this incident, the appellant explained that he later found out that his co-worker had hoped that the appellant would be fired so that his job could be given back to one of his co-worker's friends. In the end, the employer blamed the co-worker and threatened to fire him if it happened again.

I am of the opinion that not only is this is an isolated incident, but the evidence also shows that the appellant's race or nationality were not the cause of it; the appellant's co-worker wanted his friend to have the appellant's job.

In his testimony, the appellant also stated that two Haitians in his neighbourhood had been shot and killed. Here again, however, in my opinion nothing in the evidence suggests that these incidents were related to racism or discrimination, as the appellant alleged.

The RAD has taken into account the documentary evidence in the RPD's record regarding discrimination against Afro-Brazilians in Brazil (see, for example, Tab 2.1, p. 17, of the NDP for Brazil dated April 30, 2018). In addition, the appellant did not submit or cite any other documentation on this subject, either before the RPD or the RAD.

Taking into account all of the evidence presented, I arrive at the same conclusion as the RPD, namely, that the appellant has not established that the incidents he experienced and the overall situation for members of his ethnic group give rise to a well-founded fear of persecution by reason of his race, that is, a serious and repeated violation of one or more of his fundamental rights. I am also of the opinion that the appellant has not demonstrated that the discrimination he could potentially face in Brazil would make his life in that country unbearable.
In my opinion, the appellant has not established on a balance of probabilities that he would be subjected to a risk to his life, in accordance with section 97 of the IRPA.

Finally, in his memorandum, the appellant does not dispute the RPD's conclusion that he has access to state protection in Brazil. The RPD's analysis on this point is brief, and in light of my conclusions above, it is not necessary for me to further assess whether the RPD erred in its analysis.
Therefore, considering the foregoing, I conclude that the appellant has not demonstrated that the RPD made errors that warrant the RAD's intervention.

For the foregoing reasons, I confirm the RPD's determination, namely, that XXXX XXXX is not a "Convention refugee" under section 96 of the IRPA or a "person in need of protection" within the meaning of section 97 of the IRPA.

The appeal is dismissed. Normand Leduc Normand Leduc June 4, 2018 Date IRB translation Original language: French 1 RAD.25.02 (April 9, 2013) Disponible en français RAD File No. / N° de dossier de la SAR : MB8-00797 6
